title: Chemistry 11 — Chapter 3: The Solvent Question
description: A new cleaning solvent needs its safety data sheet filled out — molecular shape, polarity, and why it behaves the way it does at the molecular level.

mika.name: Ms. Mika Tan
mika.description: Says you can't predict how two substances mix until you know their shapes.

dev.name: Dev
dev.description: Assumes any molecule with polar bonds must itself be polar.

lewis_notes.name: Lewis Structure Notes
lewis_notes.description: Valence electron counts and bonding-pair rules for common molecules.

polarity_chart.name: Polarity Reference Chart
polarity_chart.description: Shape-to-polarity mapping for common molecular geometries.

elements.text: New solvent came in for testing. Before we know what it'll dissolve, we need its molecular shape, whether it's polar, and what intermolecular forces it relies on.
It's got polar bonds in it, so the whole molecule's polar, right? Case closed.

elements.prompt: Mika hands you the reference notes.

options.text: "Not necessarily — shape matters too. Let's actually work through the structure."

elements.text: Start with valence electrons. Oxygen has 6. In water, oxygen forms 2 bonding pairs (one to each hydrogen) and keeps 2 lone pairs — that's 4 electron groups total, which is why water bends instead of staying straight.

The number and arrangement of those electron groups is what VSEPR theory uses to predict shape: two bonding groups and no lone pairs gives linear, four bonding groups with no lone pairs gives tetrahedral, and so on.

config.prompt: Oxygen has 6 valence electrons and forms 2 bonding pairs in H2O. How many lone pairs are left on the oxygen atom? (just the number)
Sort each molecule by its VSEPR molecular shape.

elements.text: Here's the part people miss: a molecule can be full of polar bonds and still be nonpolar overall, if its shape is symmetric enough for the individual bond dipoles to cancel out.

CO2 has two polar C=O bonds, but it's linear and symmetric — the dipoles point in exactly opposite directions and cancel. Net result: nonpolar molecule. Water's bent shape means its two O-H dipoles don't cancel, so the molecule stays polar.

config.prompt: Sort each molecule by its overall polarity.

config.question: CO2 has two polar C=O bonds. Why is the overall molecule nonpolar?

options.text: Its linear, symmetric shape makes the two bond dipoles point in opposite directions and cancel
Carbon and oxygen actually have identical electronegativities
CO2 doesn't have any polar bonds to begin with
Double bonds are never polar regardless of the atoms involved

config.explanation: Molecular polarity depends on both bond polarity AND geometry — CO2's symmetric linear shape cancels the two C=O dipoles.

elements.text: Odd thing in the data — water boils way higher than H2S, even though sulfur is bigger and heavier than oxygen. Shouldn't the heavier molecule have the higher boiling point?

Not when hydrogen bonding is involved. Every molecule has weak London dispersion forces from momentary electron shifts. Polar molecules add stronger dipole-dipole attraction on top of that. But when hydrogen is bonded directly to nitrogen, oxygen, or fluorine, you get hydrogen bonding — the strongest intermolecular force, and it's why water's boiling point is so much higher than its size alone would predict.

config.prompt: Order these intermolecular forces from weakest to strongest.
What is the name of the intermolecular force responsible for water's unusually high boiling point?

elements.text: Shape, polarity, and dominant intermolecular force — all correctly identified. The data sheet is complete.
It's filled out, but a couple of calls were shaky. Let's double check the shape-to-polarity logic before the next sample.

elements.prompt: The data sheet is ready to file. What now?

options.text: Show Dev why 'polar bonds' and 'polar molecule' aren't the same claim, using CO2 and H2O side by side.
File it and move on. Good enough for today.

elements.text: So shape decides whether the bond dipoles cancel out or not — that's the piece I was missing. It's never just about the bonds themselves.

ending.description: Correctly worked out shape, polarity, and intermolecular forces from first principles, and corrected Dev's polar-bond assumption.
